name: Maniyaka / Liberian Mandingo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University (for Peace Corps). 183 pp. ERIC ED247767. Open full text:https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED247767.pdf
catalog_locator: Ch. IV 'Reference grammar of Maniyaka', sec. 3 'Supasegmental Features' [sic], 3.1 'Tone', p. 50; 3.31 'A Note On Timing', p. 51; Ch. VI E 'Mande suprasegmentals', 2 'Stress' and 3 'Tone', p. 166.
catalog_quote: [p. 50, 3.1 Tone] Mãniyakã is a tone language which means that two words can be distinguished from one another according to the pitch of the voice. There are a large number of words in Mãniyakã that have identical consonants and vowels but they constitute a minimal pair with respect to the tones that each has. Mãniyakã has two tones which are referred to as HIGH and LOW. ... dunu load / du̲nu rooster; so horse / so̲ town; wula afternoon / wu̲la forest. [p. 51, 3.31 A Note On Timing] Mãniyakã is a syllable-timed tongue. This means that every syllable has the same duration as every other one (long vowels are considered to be two syllables.) In English this is not the case because English is a stress-timed language. ... [p. 166, E. Mande suprasegmentals, 2. Stress] While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable, and is often accompanied by a slight increase in the length of the syllable. [3. Tone] No Mande language has more than three distinctive pitch levels. Kpelle and Mano have three: high, mid and low, while Lorma and Manya have two.

IV 'Reference grammar', '3. Supasegmental Features / 3.1 Tone': 'Mãniyakã is a tone language which means that two words can be distinguished from one another according to the pitch of the voice.. Mãniyakã has two tones which are referred to as HIGH and LOW.' with the minimal pairs dunu load/rooster, gbãgbã dust/bracelet, sẽ leg/bridge, so horse/town, wula afternoon/forest -- verbatim as quoted. (2) p. 54 = printed p. 51, '3.31 A Note On Timing': 'Mãniyakã is a syllable-timed tongue. This means that every syllable has the same duration as every other…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Manya/Maniyaka is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tonal minimal pairs and syllable-timed rhythm; the Maniyaka grammar gives no word-stress placement rule. The handbook's generic Mande chapter says stress is non-contrastive in Mande (rule illustrated only for Kpelle), and Vydrin 2017 (family overview, p. 34) states stress is absent in most Mande languages. Davydov 2017 p. 166 independently confirms Manya (with Konya) is tonal, with tone patterns inverted relative to Maninka-Mori.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Manya. Authors note 'a great deal of dialectal variation in Liberian Mandingo/Maniyaka' (grammar, p. 63) but only regarding morphology.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is lexical (word-level minimal pairs); the 'syllable-timed' remark concerns rhythm, and the only stress mentioned for Maniyaka is English-style sentence stress used as a contrast. The p. 166 stress remark is about Mande languages in general, not a Manya-specific claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Cutler & Dwyer 1981 describe 'Maniyaka' = 'Liberian Mandingo', which they equate with Manya ('Manya (also known as Mandingo) spoken in the border area between Guinea and Liberia', ch. I p. 1); this is Glottolog many1261 [mzj] (alt. names Maniya, Mandingo, Manya Kan), Liberian side of the area, with acknowledged internal dialect variation. Davydov 2017 describes Manya of Macenta (Forest Guinea) jointly with Konya/Konyanka [mku] (Glottolog subgroup kony1252 'Konya-Manya'); his tone-inversion statement is made for the Konya-Manya sub-continuum as a whole. Note the Glottolog 5.1 'glottolog_refs' list passed in our source list for this key is polluted with unrelated German 'gesprochener Sprache' titles; the live Glottolog page has only 3 refs (Heydorn, Hintze 1948, Germann 1933).

sources.note: p. 166: sub-continuum '2. Konya (and idioms gravitating to it) and Manya. Main features: inverted tonal schemes, loss of intervocalic velars.. perfective marker vɛ́ (wɛ́), 1SG pronoun mɔ́'; p. 170: most Manding idioms have two basic word tone patterns; Konya patterns are inverted relative to Maninka-Mori. Nothing on stress/accent. Based on the author's own dialect questionnaire (per Vydrin p. 19: 'Manya.. spoken in Macenta town and surrounding countryside in Forest Guinea; in many characteristics close to Konya').

sources.note: The inventory (27 segments, filterable by class consonant / tone / vowel) contains exactly two segments of class 'tone', both non-marginal: ˦ 'MODIFIER LETTER HIGH TONE BAR' (in 552 = 18% of PHOIBLE inventories) and ˨ 'MODIFIER LETTER LOW TONE BAR' (545 = 18%) - i.e. PHOIBLE codes Manya, on the basis of Manessy 1964, as having a two-level tone inventory, High vs Low, with no contour or mid tonemes; no prose on tone rules, domains or the Konya-Manya inversion (database record only). Consistent with the on-file statement from Cutler & Dwyer 1981 (two tones, HIGH and LOW).
